name: Sorani Kurdish
catalog_citation: Thackston, W. M. 2006. Sorani Kurdish: A Reference Grammar with Selected Readings. Harvard University (Iranian Studies), online PDF (via the Internet Archive 2011 capture of fas.harvard.edu/~iranian/Sorani/).
catalog_quote: Stress. All nouns and adjectives are stressed on the final syllable: tanaká ... ‘tin can,’ gawrá ... ‘big’. When enclitic endings are added, stress remains on the final syllable of the base word: tanakáyèk ... ‘a tin can,’ tanakáyèk i gawrá ... ‘a big tin can.’ The definite suffix is stressed: tanakayaká ... ‘the tin can.’ The hierarchy of stress in verbs is as follows: (1) The negative prefixes na- and nâ-, as in náchû ... ‘he didn’t go’ and nâ´che ... ‘he doesn’t go.’ (2) Preverbs like war-, hał-, and dâ-, as in wárgeřâm ... ‘I returned,’ háłdagirim ... ‘I pick up,’ and dâ´nîshtim ... ‘I sat down.’ (3) The modal prefixes (d)a- and bi- as in dábînim ... ‘I see’ and bíbînim ... ‘let me see.’ (4) When there are no prefixes on finite verbal forms, the final syllable of the verb stem is stressed, as in hâ´tin ... ‘they came’ and kírdibetmânawa ... ‘that we have opened it.’ (5) The infiniti…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote confirmed verbatim in the Thackston 2006 text we hold at Phonology 'Stress', pp. 3-4. (2) The deciding source is a 2006 unpublished Harvard teaching/reference grammar; for stress the strongest works are Hamid 2016 (dedicated Newcastle PhD on CK prosody) and McCarus 1958/1997. I downloaded Hamid 2016 (Newcastle eTheses) and McCarus 1958 (ERIC ED089545) into and read their stress sections: both agree with every coded point (final stress on the stem/prosodic word; definite -aka and plural -an stressed; indefinite -ek, ezafe, person endings stress-neutral; negative and preverb prefixes stressed in verbs; bi- usually unstressed per McCarus, which slightly qualifies Thackston's item (3)). sources.quote: p.34: 'Stress is phonemic in Kurdish, as evidenced by the pairs /morá/ 'dice' and /móra/ 'it is purple' ... The placement of loud stress is not predictable, although in general it falls on the ultima unless the ultima is an inflectional suffix. ... a word has only one loud stress; all other syllables receive weak stress, except that the pre-pretonic or the post-posttonic, if any, receives medium stress'. sources.note: Classic descriptive grammar of Sulaimani Sorani with an explicit lexical-stress section (ultima unless inflectional suffix; medium stress on pre-pretonic; negatives/preverbs stressed) that independently corroborates Thackston.

sources.citation: Hamid, Twana Saadi. 2016. The prosodic phonology of Central Kurdish. PhD thesis, Newcastle University. http://theses.ncl.ac.uk/jspui/handle/10443/3386
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p.115: 'Primary stress is final regardless to the weight of the syllable and determines the placement of secondary stress. It is usually two syllables away from primary stress (McCarus 1958, 1997; Abdulla and McCarus 1967...)'; CK 'has a binary alternating stress with primary stress assigned to the final syllable and secondary syllable on every other syllable starting from right to left'. pp.117-119: stressable suffixes (DEF -aka, PL -ân, COMP -tir) attract stress to the rightmost stressable suffix; enclitics (person markers, ezafe -i, indefinite -ek, -ish, u) 'neither attract stress nor repel
sources.note: The only dedicated prosodic study of Central Kurdish stress (foot = syllabic iamb, PWd-final primary stress, alternating secondary stress, stressable suffixes vs stress-neutral clitics); our record rests on a one-paragraph statement in an unpublished teaching grammar and says secondary stress 'None described'.
